newsitem.title: USA: UPS rivals to keep only small market share gains.
newsitem.headline: UPS rivals to keep only small market share gains.

text.p: United Parcel Service rivals may hold onto some business gained during the 15-day Teamsters strike, but none threaten to unseat UPS as the world's largest package delivery company.
UPS' overwhelming dominance in the market for "non-urgent" parcels means that customers have few choices apart from the Atlanta-based carrier, analysts said.

"Companies will likely try to find shipping alternatives so they don't get stuck in this position again, but when you control most of the market, how far can customers go?" said Steven Lewins, an analyst with Gruntal & Co.

UPS, which controls about 63 percent of the parcel delivery market, said Tuesday that it could lose about 5 percent of its annual business to competitors as a result of the strike by 185,000 Teamsters. Citing the loss of business, the company said some 15,000 union jobs may be eliminated.
UPS reached a tentative settlement with the Teamsters on Monday night after nearly 90 hours of negotiations. The company said the walkout cost it about $650 million.
The estimated losses will mean moderate gains spread among rivals such as Federal Express Corp., RPS Inc., a unit of motor freight carrier Caliber System Inc. and Airborne Freight Corp..
"Competitors have all benefited on the short-term and some may benefit over the long-term," said Douglas Rockel, an analyst with Furman Selz.
While the shippers were forced to increase spending to handle the added volume, many are likely to see a gain in third quarter earnings as a result of the strike, he said.
The biggest winner, however, could be the U.S. Postal Service.

It will take about six weeks to determine the extent of UPS' losses, but "some of the primary bread and butter business may stay with the Postal Service," said Brian Routledge, an analyst with Prudential Securities. "They are the closest (to UPS) on pricing and infrastructure," he said.
U.S. Postmaster General Marvin Runyon told CNBC on Tuesday that package volume during the strike came close to peak holiday levels.
Demand for overnight service jumped 70 percent, while 2- to 3-day deliveries rose 50 percent. In the last few days of the strike, regular parcel post volume surged 50 percent.

The Postal Service said it hired 4,700 temporary workers and increased overtime hours for its regular workers by about 50 percent. But Runyon said it was too early to tell whether the Postal Service would retain the new customers.
"It's kind of like they've been on a date with us a couple of times," Runyon told CNBC.

Meanwhile, FedEx said its business increased 35 percent to 40 percent above the normal 2.8 million packages it handles each day. The Memphis-based priority delivery company said it turned away business to avoid over-stretching its operations.
"There will be some short-term financial benefit, but the long-term is hard to tell," said Shirlee Clark, a spokeswoman for FedEx.
Since FedEx handled many packages during the strike that do not fall into its typical priority delivery market, the company did not expect to retain much of that business.
"The large percentage of what people were asking us to handle were packages that would normally go by the parcel post ... that don't have time-sensitive need," Clark said.
Much of the long-term gains for rivals depend on UPS' pricing and service strategy as it emerges from the strike, analysts said.
Since UPS is already the low-cost shipper and faces minimal competition in the small parcel sector, the company is not likely to trim costs in that market.
But the company may have to offer price breaks in the heavier-weight package market in order to win back customers, analysts said. UPS did not return calls seeking comment.
